entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11464"/><div sID="gen20744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11464"/><hi type="bold">3. pot--</hi>caldron. Alluding to the self-confident proverb used among the people, <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.3">Eze 11:3</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.3">Eze 11:3</reference>), "This city is the caldron and we be the flesh"; your proverb shall prove awfully true, but in a different sense from what you intend. So far from the city proving an iron, caldron-like defense from the fire, it shall be as a caldron set on the fire, and the people as so many pieces of meat subjected to boiling heat. See <reference osisRef="Jer.1.13">Jr 1:13</reference>. <div eID="gen20744" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11468"/><div sID="gen20752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11468"/><hi type="bold">7. upon the top of a rock--</hi>or, "the dry, bare, exposed rock," so as to be conspicuous to all. Blood poured on a rock is not so soon absorbed as blood poured on the earth. The law ordered the blood even of a beast or fowl to be "covered with the dust" (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.13">Le 17:13</reference>); but Jerusalem was so shameless as to be at no pains to cover up the blood of innocent men slain in her. Blood, as the consummation of all sin, presupposes every other form of guilt. <div eID="gen20752" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11477"/><div sID="gen20764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11477"/><hi type="bold">16. desire of ... eyes--</hi>his wife: representing the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>) in which the Jews so much gloried. The energy and subordination of Ezekiel's whole life to his prophetic office is strikingly displayed in this narrative of his wife's death. It is the only memorable event of his personal history which he records, and this only in reference to his soul-absorbing work. His natural tenderness is shown by that graphic touch, "the desire of thine eyes." What amazing subjection, then, of his individual feeling to his prophetic duty is manifested in the simple statement (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.18">Eze 24:18</reference>), "So I spake ... in the morning; and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded."<div eID="gen20764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stroke--</hi>a sudden visitation. The suddenness of it enhances the self-control of Ezekiel in so entirely merging individual feeling, which must have been especially acute under such trying circumstances, in the higher claims of duty to God. <div eID="gen20765" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11478"/><div sID="gen20766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11478"/><hi type="bold">17. Forbear to cry--</hi>or, "Lament in silence"; not forbidding sorrow, but the loud expression of it [Grotius].<div eID="gen20766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no mourning--</hi>typical of the universality of the ruin of Jerusalem, which would preclude mourning, such as is usual where calamity is but partial. "The dead" is purposely put in the plural, as referring ultimately to the dead who should perish at the taking of Jerusalem; though the singular might have been expected, as Ezekiel's wife was the immediate subject referred to: "make no mourning," such as is usual, "for the dead, and such as shall be hereafter in Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.5-Jer.16.7">Jr 16:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen20767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tire of thine head--</hi>thy headdress [Fairbairn]. Jerome explains, "Thou shalt retain the hair which is usually cut in mourning." The fillet, binding the hair about the temples like a chaplet, was laid aside at such times. Uncovering the head was an ordinary sign of mourning in priests; whereas others covered their heads in mourning (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>). The reason was, the priests had their headdress of fine twined linen given them for ornament, and as a badge of office. The high priest, as having on his head the holy anointing oil, was forbidden in any case to lay aside his headdress. But the priests might do so in the case of the death of the nearest relatives (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.2">Le 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.3.10">3, 10</reference>). They then put on inferior attire, sprinkling also on their heads dust and ashes (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.10.6">Le 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen20768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shoes upon thy feet--</hi>whereas mourners went "barefoot" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>).<div eID="gen20769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cover not ... lips--</hi>rather, the "upper lip," with the moustache (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Le 13:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.7">Mi 3:7</reference>).<div eID="gen20770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bread of men--</hi>the bread usually brought to mourners by friends in token of sympathy. So the "cup of consolation" brought (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.7">Jr 16:7</reference>). "Of men" means such as is usually furnished by men. So <reference osisRef="Isa.8.1">Is 8:1</reference>, "a man's pen"; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.17">Re 21:17</reference>, "the measure of a man." <div eID="gen20771" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 17. Forbear to cry-- or, "Lament in silence"; not forbidding sorrow, but the loud expression of it [Grotius]. no mourning-- typical of the universality of the ruin of Jerusalem, which would preclude mourning, such as is usual where calamity is but partial. "The dead" is purposely put in the plural, as referring ultimately to the dead who should perish at the taking of Jerusalem; though the singular might have been expected, as Ezekiel's wife was the immediate subject referred to: "make no mourning," such as is usual, "for the dead, and such as shall be hereafter in Jerusalem" ( Jr 16:5-7 ). tire of thine head-- thy headdress [Fairbairn]. Jerome explains, "Thou shalt retain the hair which is usually cut in mourning." The fillet, binding the hair about the temples like a chaplet, was laid aside at such times. Uncovering the head was an ordinary sign of mourning in priests; whereas others covered their heads in mourning ( 2Sa 15:30 ). The reason was, the priests had their headdress of fine twined linen given them for ornament, and as a badge of office. The high priest, as having on his head the holy anointing oil, was forbidden in any case to lay aside his headdress. But the priests might do so in the case of the death of the nearest relatives ( Le 21:2 , 3, 10 ). They then put on inferior attire, sprinkling also on their heads dust and ashes (compare Le 10:6 , 7 ). shoes upon thy feet-- whereas mourners went "barefoot" ( 2Sa 15:30 ). cover not ... lips-- rather, the "upper lip," with the moustache ( Le 13:45 ; Mi 3:7 ). bread of men-- the bread usually brought to mourners by friends in token of sympathy. So the "cup of consolation" brought ( Jr 16:7 ). "Of men" means such as is usually furnished by men. So Is 8:1 , "a man's pen"; Re 21:17 , "the measure of a man."
entries.reader_content_plain: 17. Forbear to cry-- or, "Lament in silence"; not forbidding sorrow, but the loud expression of it [Grotius]. no mourning-- typical of the universality of the ruin of Jerusalem, which would preclude mourning, such as is usual where calamity is but partial. "The dead" is purposely put in the plural, as referring ultimately to the dead who should perish at the taking of Jerusalem; though the singular might have been expected, as Ezekiel's wife was the immediate subject referred to: "make no mourning," such as is usual, "for the dead, and such as shall be hereafter in Jerusalem" ( Jr 16:5-7 ). tire of thine head-- thy headdress [Fairbairn]. Jerome explains, "Thou shalt retain the hair which is usually cut in mourning." The fillet, binding the hair about the temples like a chaplet, was laid aside at such times. Uncovering the head was an ordinary sign of mourning in priests; whereas others covered their heads in mourning ( 2Sa 15:30 ). The reason was, the priests had their headdress of fine twined linen given them for ornament, and as a badge of office. The high priest, as having on his head the holy anointing oil, was forbidden in any case to lay aside his headdress. But the priests might do so in the case of the death of the nearest relatives ( Le 21:2 , 3, 10 ). They then put on inferior attire, sprinkling also on their heads dust and ashes (compare Le 10:6 , 7 ). shoes upon thy feet-- whereas mourners went "barefoot" ( 2Sa 15:30 ). cover not ... lips-- rather, the "upper lip," with the moustache ( Le 13:45 ; Mi 3:7 ). bread of men-- the bread usually brought to mourners by friends in token of sympathy. So the "cup of consolation" brought ( Jr 16:7 ). "Of men" means such as is usually furnished by men. So Is 8:1 , "a man's pen"; Re 21:17 , "the measure of a man."

They could not in their exile manifest publicly their lamentation, but they would privately "mourn one to another." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11484"/><div sID="gen20782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11484"/>25-26. "The day" referred to in these verses is the day of the overthrow of the temple, when the fugitive "escapes." But "that day," in <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.27">Eze 24:27</reference>, is the day on which the fugitive brings the sad news to Ezekiel, at the Chebar. In the interval the prophet suspended his prophecies as to the Jews, as was foretold.
